questions.question: Explain the meaning of realism in Indian New Wave Cinema. / [CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain the meaning of realism in Indian New Wave Cinema. [U] / [CO4]
  • • Represents everyday life and social realities with a sense of authenticity.
  • • Often focuses on ordinary people and marginalized communities.
  • • Addresses issues such as poverty, caste, gender, and inequality.
  • • Frequently uses naturalistic acting, locations, and restrained visual style.

questions.question: What is meant by the term auteur in the context of French New Wave cinema? / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• What is meant by the term auteur in the context of French New Wave cinema? [U] / [CO2]
  • • An auteur is a filmmaker whose personal vision is evident in their films.
  • • The director is treated as a major creative force behind the film.
  • • Recurring themes, visual choices, and narrative approaches express the director’s style.
  • • French New Wave directors such as François Truffaut and Jean-Luc Godard are commonly associated with
  • auteur theory.

questions.question: Analyse the development of the star system during the Golden Age. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Analyse the development of the star system during the Golden Age. [An] / [CO3]
  • • The studio system developed and promoted actors as recognisable stars.
  • • Studios shaped star images through publicity, contracts, interviews, and carefully selected roles.
  • • Stars helped attract audiences and contributed to a film’s commercial success.
  • • Genre roles and recurring screen personas made stars familiar to viewers.
  • • Fan magazines, posters, and other publicity strengthened their popularity.
  • • The system often limited actors’ freedom to choose roles or control their public image.
  • • The star system linked celebrity, studio power, and audience identification.

questions.question: Explain the importance of representation in contemporary Indian cinema. / [CO5]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain the importance of representation in contemporary Indian cinema. [U] / [CO5]
  • • Representation shapes how communities, identities, and social experiences are seen on screen.
  • • It can increase the visibility of groups historically underrepresented in mainstream cinema.
  • • Films can challenge stereotypes related to caste, class, gender, region, disability, and religion.
  • • Authentic representation can make stories more inclusive and relatable.
  • • Characters and narratives influence public understanding and social attitudes.
  • • Contemporary cinema includes diverse voices and perspectives, though gaps remain.
  • • Responsible representation requires attention to whose stories are told and how.

questions.question: Discuss how genre conventions can be modified or combined to transform film form. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Discuss how genre conventions can be modified or combined to transform film form. [U] / [CO1]
  • • Genre conventions are familiar themes, characters, settings, and narrative patterns.
  • • Filmmakers can alter expected plot structures or character roles to create surprise.
  • • Combining genres can produce hybrid forms, such as comedy-drama or science-fiction thriller.
  • • Subverting conventions can challenge audience expectations and established meanings.
  • • Changes in cinematography, editing, sound, and performance can reshape genre style.
  • • Genre experimentation can reflect new cultural contexts and audience interests.
  • • Give a relevant film example to illustrate modification or genre blending.

questions.question: Apply the idea of self-reflexivity to explain how a film can draw attention to its own construction and conventions. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Apply the idea of self-reflexivity to explain how a film can draw attention to its own construction and
  • conventions. [A] / [CO2]
  • • Self-reflexivity occurs when a film makes viewers aware that they are watching a constructed work.
  • • It may reveal cameras, filmmaking processes, editing, or performance within the story.
  • • Characters may acknowledge the audience or comment on familiar film conventions.
  • • The film may interrupt conventional continuity or expose how its narrative is made.
  • • Such techniques encourage viewers to question realism and cinematic illusion.
  • • Self-reflexivity can create humour, criticism, or intellectual distance.
  • • Examples may include films about filmmaking or works that deliberately expose their own artifice.

questions.question: Describe the Lumière brothers and state its significance. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Describe the Lumière brothers and state their significance. [K] / [CO1]
  • • Auguste and Louis Lumière were French inventors and pioneers of early cinema.
  • • They developed the Cinématographe, which could function as a camera, printer, and projector.
  • • They organised public film screenings in Paris in December 1895.
  • • Their films often recorded brief scenes of everyday life.
  • • Workers Leaving the Lumière Factory and Arrival of a Train at La Ciotat are well-known examples.
  • • Their screenings helped establish cinema as a public entertainment and exhibition medium.
  • • Their work was important to the early development of documentary-style moving images.

questions.question: Evaluate whether Parallel Cinema is necessarily realistic. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Evaluate whether Parallel Cinema is necessarily realistic. [E] / [CO3]
  • • Parallel Cinema often addresses social realities and experiences overlooked by mainstream cinema.
  • • It frequently uses naturalistic acting, real locations, and understated storytelling.
  • • Many films examine poverty, caste, gender, rural life, and political structures.
  • • However, realism is a tendency rather than an absolute rule.
  • • Parallel Cinema can use symbolism, stylisation, allegory, non-linear narratives, or poetic imagery.
  • • Filmmakers may interpret reality rather than reproduce it exactly.
  • • Therefore, Parallel Cinema is often socially grounded but is not necessarily realistic in every film or
  • technique.

questions.question: Evaluate the use of AI in filmmaking. / [CO5] [5x6 = 30]
questions.solution_html:
• Evaluate the use of AI in filmmaking. [E] / [CO5]
  • • AI can support script development, storyboarding, pre-visualisation, and production planning.
  • • It can assist with editing, subtitles, dubbing, visual effects, and restoration.
  • • AI tools may reduce time and costs for selected tasks.
  • • They raise concerns about authorship, originality, consent, copyright, and the use of training data.
  • • AI-generated likenesses or voices can create risks for performers and their livelihoods.
  • • Human judgement remains important for creative decisions, context, and ethical responsibility.
  • • Evaluation should balance creative and practical benefits against labour, legal, and ethical concerns.
  • [5 × 6 = 30]

questions.question: Examine how the introduction of synchronized sound changed film form and style. Discuss dialogue, sound effects, music, acting, editing, camera movement and staging. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Examine how the introduction of synchronized sound changed film form and style. Discuss dialogue,
  • sound effects, music, acting, editing, camera movement and staging. [U] / [CO1]
  • • Synchronized sound linked recorded voices and sounds to the images on screen.
  • • Dialogue became a major means of conveying character, information, and plot.
  • • Sound effects increased the sense of physical presence and helped construct believable environments.
  • • Music could accompany action, establish mood, and guide emotional responses.
  • • Acting styles changed as vocal expression, diction, and timing became important.
  • • Early sound recording often restricted camera movement because microphones and recording equipment
  • were less flexible.
  • QP Code : 26900380
  • • Staging adapted to microphone placement and the need to capture clear dialogue.
  • • Editing practices changed as filmmakers coordinated image cuts with dialogue, music, and sound continuity.
  • • Some early sound films used longer takes and less mobile camera setups.
  • • Sound enabled new genres and performance traditions, including the dialogue-driven drama and the
  • musical.
  • • Cinema developed techniques such as sound bridges, off-screen sound, and more complex sound-image
  • relationships.
  • • The transition was gradual; filmmakers experimented with ways to integrate sound rather than simply record
  • dialogue.
  • • Overall, synchronized sound transformed narrative, performance, technical practice, and cinematic style.

questions.question: Examine how New Hollywood transformed traditional genre conventions. Discuss revisionist Westerns, crime films, road films and other genres in relation to changing American cultural contexts. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Examine how New Hollywood transformed traditional genre conventions. Discuss revisionist
  • Westerns, crime films, road films and other genres in relation to changing American cultural contexts.
  • [A] / [CO2]
  • • New Hollywood emerged mainly in the late 1960s and 1970s amid social and political change in the United
  • States.
  • • Filmmakers challenged the polished storytelling and moral certainty associated with classical Hollywood.
  • • Antiheroes and morally ambiguous characters replaced many traditional heroic figures.
  • • Revisionist Westerns questioned the myth of the frontier and often presented violence and expansion
  • critically.
  • • Crime films explored corruption, alienation, institutional failure, and the costs of power.
  • • Road films used journeys to explore freedom, rebellion, identity, and disillusionment.
  • • Other genres blended conventions or used unconventional narrative structures and endings.
  • • More explicit violence, sexuality, and social conflict reflected changing censorship and audience
  • expectations.
  • • Location shooting, naturalistic performances, and experimental editing helped create a more immediate
  • style.
  • • Films responded to the Vietnam War, civil rights struggles, counterculture, and distrust of authority.
  • • Examples may include Bonnie and Clyde, The Wild Bunch, Easy Rider, and Chinatown, with relevant
  • explanation.
  • • Not every film rejected classical conventions; many combined innovation with familiar genre structures.
  • • New Hollywood renewed genres by making them more ambiguous, critical, and responsive to contemporary
  • culture.

questions.question: Evaluate the importance of Alam Ara in the transition from silent cinema to sound cinema. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Evaluate the importance of Alam Ara in the transition from silent cinema to sound cinema. [E] /
  • [CO3]
  • • Alam Ara was directed by Ardeshir Irani and released in 1931.
  • • It is widely recognised as India’s first full-length talkie.
  • • Its release marked a major turning point in Indian film production and exhibition.
  • • Dialogue became audible as part of the narrative rather than being conveyed only through intertitles or
  • gestures.
  • • Songs and music became central features of Indian popular cinema.
  • • The film helped establish a model in which music, performance, and storytelling were closely connected.
  • • Actors and filmmakers had to adapt to new demands of voice, diction, recording, and sound staging.
  • • Production companies invested in sound recording equipment and new technical practices.
  • • Regional-language talkies followed, expanding sound cinema across India’s linguistic communities.
  • • The shift affected acting styles, scripts, studio practices, and audience expectations.
  • QP Code : 26900380
  • • Sound also brought challenges, including technical limitations and changes in the kinds of performances that
  • could be recorded effectively.
  • • Alam Ara’s historical significance is clear even though the film itself is now considered lost.
  • • It helped initiate the sound era in Indian cinema and shaped later popular film conventions.

questions.question: Critically examine the relationship between technology and the changing aesthetics of Indian cinema. / [CO4] [15x2 = 30]
questions.solution_html:
• Critically examine the relationship between technology and the changing aesthetics of Indian cinema.
  • [E] / [CO4]
  • • Technological changes influence how Indian films are produced, distributed, and experienced.
  • • The arrival of synchronized sound transformed dialogue, music, performance, and narrative style.
  • • Colour processes expanded visual expression and changed the use of costume, setting, lighting, and
  • spectacle.
  • • Improvements in cameras, lenses, lighting, and film stock broadened cinematographic possibilities.
  • • Portable equipment and location recording supported more naturalistic and independent filmmaking.
  • • Digital cinematography reduced some production barriers and enabled new visual styles.
  • • Computer-generated imagery and visual effects expanded the possibilities of spectacle and imagined worlds.
  • • Digital editing enabled faster workflows, complex structures, and precise control over rhythm and
  • continuity.
  • • Streaming platforms and digital distribution changed access, viewing habits, and the circulation of regional
  • and independent films.
  • • Mobile phones and affordable digital tools have opened new opportunities for emerging filmmakers.
  • • Technology can support experimentation but does not automatically produce artistic quality or originality.
  • • Access to expensive tools remains unequal, and technological dependence can affect labour and production
  • practices.
  • • Indian cinema’s aesthetics develop through the interaction of technology with culture, creative choices,
  • audience expectations, and social context.
  • [15 × 2 = 30]
